description: The Crystalline Bloom drifts through space as an impossible garden of geometric perfection. Millions of crystalline structures ranging from meter-scale shards to kilometer-long spires float in loose formation, their surfaces refracting starlight into prismatic cascades of color. The formations appear to grow from nothing, adding measurable mass without any detectable source material, defying conservation laws that govern normal matter.

The crystals respond to electromagnetic energy with subtle but measurable growth acceleration. Ships passing through report their hulls becoming hosts to crystalline seeds within hours, the formations spreading along power conduits and communication lines with apparent purpose. The growth is not malicious—it simply is, following rules that materials scientists have yet to fully decode. Removal requires specialized equipment; the crystals bond at a molecular level.

No record exists of the Bloom's discovery—it appears in navigation charts dating back to the earliest human expansion, always in approximately the same region, though its slow expansion has been documented over centuries. Analysis of the crystals reveals structures impossible to replicate in laboratories: perfect lattices with zero defects, isotopic ratios found nowhere else in the galaxy. Some researchers believe the Bloom is not an anomaly but an organism, or perhaps a machine, growing according to programming written before Earth's sun ignited.

The Consortium of Material Sciences maintains a heavily shielded research station at the Bloom's edge, harvesting samples that command extraordinary prices for their unique properties. Ship captains willing to risk crystal contamination can earn substantial salvage fees retrieving samples from deep within the formation. The greater mystery remains unsolved: the Bloom is expanding at 3.2 kilometers per century, and trajectory analysis suggests it will eventually reach inhabited systems. Whether this represents a threat or an opportunity remains hotly debated.
